title: Maritime NDT Audit Support: IACS Class Approval Audits
description: Level III support for IACS UR Z17 and UR W35 class approval audits: procedures, operator files, calibration records and mock audits. Ask about your audit.
h1: Maritime NDT Audit Support: Preparing for IACS Class Approval Audits
html:
This page is for thickness measurement firms, NDT service suppliers, shipyards, repair yards and offshore fabricators that face a class society audit of their NDT: an initial approval, a renewal, a surveyor's review of new-construction testing, or an owner's audit of a gauging contractor. Atlantis NDT puts an ASNT NDT Level III on your procedures, operator files, calibration records and reports, runs the audit on you before the society does, and helps you close whatever it finds. To get started, send us the audit notice or the society's request.

Which maritime audit is coming?

Marine NDT answers to several audit regimes at once, and each one is prepared for differently. Pin down which regime applies before anyone rewrites a procedure, because a document set built for the wrong audit can look complete and still miss what the auditor came to check.

AuditWho carries it outGoverning requirementWhat triggers it
Initial approval as a service supplierThe class society you apply toIACS UR Z17 plus that society's own approval schemeYou want class surveyors to accept your thickness measurements, in-water survey, ultrasonic tightness testing of closing appliances or remote inspection results
Renewal of a service supplier approvalThe same societyUR Z17 section 6.2Thickness measurement firms renew at intervals not exceeding three years; most other categories at intervals not exceeding five years; a society may add intermediate audits
Verification of an NDT service supplier for new constructionThe class society, by a method it choosesIACS UR W35, with UR W33 and W34 setting the extent of hull weld testingYour firm, or your yard's in-house NDT department, tests hull structure on a classed newbuild
Surveyor review during a build or repairThe attending class surveyorSociety rules and the agreed NDT planAny classed project; the surveyor can ask for the record behind any report
Naval work reviewThe Navy's supervising authority or the prime shipbuilderThe NAVSEA technical publications named in the contractNavy new construction or repair, where class rules do not govern the testing
Owner, manager or charterer auditThe owner's technical team or a vetting partyThe contract and the owner's checklistPre-qualifying a gauging firm, a condition assessment, or a dispute over steel renewal figures

Many firms face two or three of these in the same year. A repair yard can hold a thickness measurement approval for in-service ships, be verified under UR W35 for a newbuild block contract, and host an owner's audit during a docking, each with a different evidence trail.

Where Atlantis stands: going through the same class audits

Atlantis is in the process of obtaining IACS UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS. In practice that means Atlantis is assembling the same document pack, preparing for the same office audits and planning the same witnessed demonstrations described on this page. It holds no class approval yet, and nothing here should be read as a claim that it does. Until a society issues a certificate, any thickness readings Atlantis takes support the owner's own decisions, not a class survey.

We state this plainly for two reasons. The society alone decides who is approved, so no consultant can sell you that outcome. And our advice comes from working through the requirements against a real quality system rather than from summaries of them. Atlantis is not a class society, does not audit on behalf of one, and is not a certification body. The clause-by-clause content of UR Z17, from the document pack to cancellation, is set out in our IACS UR Z17 service supplier requirements guide. This page is about getting ready for the audit itself and getting through it.

What a class auditor examines in a service supplier

Every society runs its own scheme, but each one implements UR Z17, so the evidence requested follows a common pattern. The process opens with a document review, moves to an office audit that tests whether the firm actually works the way its documents say, and ends with a witnessed demonstration of the service backed by a satisfactory report. A renewal audit asks whether those conditions held in the years since approval. Expect the auditor to open these records:

  • The quality system. A code of conduct, equipment maintenance and calibration, training programmes, supervision and verification, recording and reporting, control of agents and subcontractors, job preparation, and periodic review of complaints, corrective actions and document control. A generic ISO 9001 manual rarely covers every one of those headings without editing. See the NDT section of a UR Z17 quality manual.
  • Personnel files. UR Z17 asks for at least one year of tutored on-the-job training for each operator and at least two years of experience for the responsible supervisor, with education, training and experience recorded for every person named. For thickness measurement, the Annex 1 requirements add a responsible supervisor qualified to Level II and operators qualified to at least Level I under a recognised NDT certification scheme, plus documented knowledge of ship structure. Our page on UTM operator qualification for class approval explains how these files usually fall short.
  • Equipment records. Every gauge and probe with its maintenance history, its calibration certificate and the verification checks made on a reference block before and after each job. An annual certificate on its own does not show that a gauge was reading correctly on the day. See calibration records for UR Z17.
  • Reports. Issued in a form the society accepts, with a copy of the Certificate of Approval attached once you hold one. Hull thickness reports follow the formats in the IACS UR Z7 and Z10 series, and the attending surveyor verifies each separate job.
  • Subcontracting. UR Z17 requires subcontractors that deliver the approved service to meet its general requirements too, and the firm must disclose them and control their quality. Supplied operators belong inside your system, trained on your procedures and using your forms.
  • Disclosures. Conflicts of interest, the record of customer claims, and corrective actions requested by certification bodies. An empty complaints log tends to be read as a log nobody keeps.

How DNV, ABS and Lloyd's Register run their schemes

Approval is granted one society at a time. A certificate from one society does not let your readings be credited on a ship classed by another, so a firm that gauges for several fleets usually carries several approvals, each with its own audit trail and renewal date. The three societies whose approval Atlantis is pursuing handle it as follows.

  • DNV approves service suppliers under its class programme DNV-CP-0484. Its certificates name the type of service, a scope category and an expiry date, and list the grounds for withdrawal, such as deficiencies a surveyor finds in the supplier's working systems or a failure to report major changes. DNV also prescribes its own reporting tool for thickness measurement on ships in service. More detail is on our page about DNV approval of service suppliers.
  • ABS calls the firms it recognises External Specialists. Its service categories follow the UR Z17 types, beginning with thickness measurement on ships and mobile offshore units, with the same exclusion for non-ESP ships under 500 gross tonnage and all fishing vessels. See the ABS service supplier requirements and the personnel records ABS auditors ask for.
  • Lloyd's Register operates its own approval scheme for service suppliers under the same IACS requirement, with its own application route, audit and certificate.

IACS members also share the status of thickness measurement firms. Under IACS Procedural Requirement PR 23, members report new approvals, expiries, suspensions and cancellations to a common record and consult it before issuing or renewing a certificate. UR Z17 lets a society cancel an approval for work improperly performed or reported, for deficiencies a surveyor finds that are not corrected, for missed intermediate audits, and for wilful acts or deliberate misrepresentation. A cancellation by one society is therefore visible to the others, which is why a sloppy renewal can cost far more than one certificate.

New construction NDT and shipyard audits

Testing on a classed newbuild sits under a different requirement. IACS UR W35 covers NDT service suppliers working on hull structure and related items during new construction, including the in-house NDT departments of shipyards and block fabricators, and it takes those firms out of the scope of UR Z17. Each society decides how it verifies a supplier under W35, so one society may audit your office while another reviews your documents and samples your reports on the job.

Three W35 points regularly catch US firms. The written practice must be acceptable to the society, and an employer-based written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A is accepted only after the society reviews it against ISO 9712; a document that names no responsible Level III, or that has never been sent to the society, will not pass. NDT procedures must be approved by your Level 3 and must take their acceptance criteria from the society's rules, not from AWS D1.1 or an ASME code. And the quality system must define who may sign a report at each certification level. Our page on maritime NDT consulting under UR W35 walks through those clauses.

Alongside W35, IACS UR W33 sets the minimum extent and acceptance of conventional NDT on hull steel welds in new construction, and UR W34 deals with advanced methods such as phased array and TOFD. Many yards and surveyors still refer to the older IACS Recommendation 20 when they agree scope. The attending surveyor works from the NDT plan the yard and the society agreed, and may ask for the evidence behind any report: the procedure revision, the technician's certificate and vision record on that date, the instrument check and the raw data. For production yards, our Level III audit support for shipbuilding and repair yards covers the build side in more depth.

Navy work follows NAVSEA requirements, not class rules

US Navy new construction and repair is a separate regime. NDT on naval work follows the NAVSEA technical publications the contract names, most often T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, Requirements for Nondestructive Testing Methods. That publication covers how radiographic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant, ultrasonic, eddy current and visual examinations are performed and the minimum requirements for qualifying the people who perform them. It does not contain acceptance criteria; those come from the governing specification, contract or order. Firms moving from commercial to naval work sometimes carry over habits, such as recertifying people on accumulated experience instead of examination, that naval requirements do not accept. Confirm the revision your contract invokes and map your written practice against it line by line.

Atlantis can carry out that mapping, review NDT procedures against the publication, and prepare personnel files for the prime's or the Navy's review. A class approval carries no weight on navy work, and a NAVSEA-compliant programme does not earn class approval either. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, where that work is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules; as a Level III it can still review radiographs and RT procedures produced by your licensed contractor. Background is in our article on NDT for naval shipbuilding.

Where maritime audits usually break

Most findings in maritime NDT audits are not technical. The work was competent; the record cannot prove it. These are the breaks a mock audit should hunt for before the society does:

  • An operator's certificate or vision record expired partway through a contract, and the renewal is dated after the job.
  • A gauge holds an annual calibration certificate but shows no recorded check on a reference block at the start and end of the measurement session.
  • Readings on coated plate were taken without recording the instrument mode, so nobody can show the coating was excluded from the figure.
  • Reported figures cannot be traced back to a field sheet that places each reading on a named structural member.
  • The report reached the owner before the attending surveyor verified the job, or it went out without the Certificate of Approval copy.
  • Operators supplied by another company worked to that company's procedures and forms instead of yours.
  • The job went beyond the scope or category printed on the certificate.
  • Procedures carry revision dates bunched into the weeks before the audit, and the field staff have never read them.
  • Someone diarised the renewal on a five-year cycle when the thickness measurement certificate runs for three.
  • A supervisor signed reports for jobs that supervisor neither attended nor reviewed.

Every item on that list surfaces when three completed jobs, picked at random, are traced from contract to signed report. That is how a society auditor samples, and it is how we run a mock audit. Qualification gaps usually lead back to the written practice, so see also NDT vision examination records and catching technician certifications before they expire.

How a maritime audit-support engagement runs

  1. Scope. You send the audit notice or the society's request, your current documents and the list of services and societies involved. We confirm which requirement governs each service and what the auditor is likely to sample.
  2. Gap review. An ASNT NDT Level III reads your quality manual, written practice, procedures, operator files, equipment records and recent reports against UR Z17 or UR W35, the society's scheme and your contracts, then returns a finding list ranked by audit risk.
  3. Documents. We revise or draft what is missing: the written practice to SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, whichever your contracts name, with the comparison the society asks for; the thickness measurement or NDT procedure; the operator guide, job checklists and report templates in the society's format; and the training programme with its on-the-job log. See NDT written practice development.
  4. Personnel files. We sort each operator's training, experience, examination, vision and certification evidence and show what is missing. Missing evidence is never recreated after the fact; where a record does not exist, your certifying Level III decides on retraining, re-examination or a limit on scope, and that decision is recorded.
  5. Mock audit. We run the office audit and a job trace on real completed work, then rehearse the witnessed demonstration: reference-block verification, readings on coated and corroded plate, location records and the finished report. Our page on procedure demonstrations explains how a demonstration is planned and recorded.
  6. Finding closure. After the real audit we help you write root cause and corrective action and assemble the objective evidence the society wants, following the approach in corrective action records for UR Z17.

Most document work is done remotely from Houston and Hyderabad. Mock audits and demonstration rehearsals take place at your office or yard. Anoop Rayavarapu, who founded Atlantis, leads the work; he holds ASNT NDT Level III certification in five methods (ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant and visual testing) and brings 11+ years of field work on several continents. Your company keeps every decision that belongs to it: you certify your own people, you own your quality system, and the society decides on approval. Operators who need method training first can take SNT-TC-1A-based maritime NDT training, although the employer still certifies them and class still expects ship-structure knowledge that no method course supplies on its own.

Owner and charterer audits of gauging firms

Class is not the only party that audits a thickness measurement firm. Owners and managers pre-qualify gauging contractors before a docking or a condition assessment, and charterers and vetting parties sometimes ask to see the evidence behind a ship's thickness records. These audits are contractual, so their scope is whatever the owner writes into the checklist. They tend to concentrate on three questions: does the firm hold the approval this ship's class requires, can its readings be traced to locations and to a verified instrument, and do its steel renewal estimates agree with the data. A firm with a clean class audit trail usually answers all three quickly. Atlantis also takes owner-side gauging work that is not credited to class, described on our ship ultrasonic thickness measurement page.

What to send us

  • The audit notice, the society's letter or the owner's checklist, with the audit date.
  • The services and societies involved, and the scope you hold or are applying for.
  • Your quality manual, NDT written practice and the procedures used for that scope.
  • The operator and supervisor list, with certificates, vision records and training and experience logs.
  • The equipment list with calibration certificates and a sample of daily verification records.
  • Three recently completed jobs with their field sheets and final reports.
  • Findings from earlier audits and the corrective actions that closed them.

Use the maritime audit enquiry form; we reply within one business day. If your certificates and expiry dates live in spreadsheets, the certificate tracking app keeps them in one place, and the guide on equipment past its calibration date covers the instrument side.

Maritime audit support at US ports

Local pages describe the shipyards, repair yards and offshore fabrication around each port and the regimes that apply there: North Charleston, Ingleside, Portsmouth, Virginia, Newport News, Groton, Bath, Maine, Lake Charles, Houma, Brownsville and Panama City. Atlantis has no office at any of these ports. It sends a Level III for the site work and handles the rest remotely. For the audit checklist in compact form, see UR Z17 audit preparation.

faq.q: Can Atlantis get our firm approved by a class society?
faq.a: No consultant can do that. The society reviews your documents, audits your office and witnesses a demonstration, and it alone decides. Atlantis prepares your documents and records, runs a mock audit and helps you close findings, so the firm you present is the firm the auditor finds.

Not yet. Atlantis is in the process of obtaining IACS UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS. Until a certificate is issued, readings Atlantis takes are for the owner's own decisions and are not credited to a class survey.

faq.q: Does a DNV approval let us measure on an ABS-classed ship?
faq.a: No. Approval is granted by each society for its own classed ships. A firm working across fleets usually holds separate approvals, each with its own audits and renewal date. The UR Z17 requirements guide covers how that works.

faq.q: How often are thickness measurement firms re-audited?
faq.a: UR Z17 sets renewal for thickness measurement firms at intervals not exceeding three years, against five years for most other service categories. A society can set shorter intervals and require intermediate audits, and missing one is grounds for cancellation.

faq.q: Will an SNT-TC-1A written practice satisfy the society?
faq.a: It depends on the requirement. For in-service thickness measurement, UR Z17 asks for operators qualified under a recognised scheme. For new-construction NDT under UR W35, the society reviews an employer-based written practice against ISO 9712 before accepting it. Ask the society early and keep its reply on file.

faq.q: What qualification do our thickness measurement operators need?
faq.a: The UR Z17 Annex 1 requirements call for a responsible supervisor qualified to Level II and operators qualified to at least Level I under a recognised NDT certification scheme, with documented knowledge of ship structure, one year of tutored on-the-job training per operator and two years of experience for the supervisor.

faq.q: Can we use operators supplied by another company?
faq.a: Yes, if you disclose the subcontracting and the supplied people meet the same requirements as your own staff. They should work to your procedures, be trained on your system and appear in your personnel records. See subcontractor approval audits.

faq.q: What happens if the auditor raises findings?
faq.a: You answer each with root cause, correction and objective evidence by the date the society sets. Deficiencies left uncorrected, improperly reported work and misrepresentation are all listed in UR Z17 as grounds for cancelling an approval. Atlantis helps you build the evidence, but the response is signed by your company.

faq.q: Does UR Z17 apply to NDT on new construction?
faq.a: No. NDT service suppliers on new construction, including yard NDT departments, are covered by IACS UR W35, which takes them out of UR Z17. Thickness measurement on ships in service stays under UR Z17.

faq.q: Do you support Navy shipbuilding and repair audits?
faq.a: Yes, on the documentation side. Atlantis maps your written practice and procedures against the NAVSEA technical publication your contract names and prepares personnel files for review. Navy work follows NAVSEA requirements, not class rules, and Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States.

faq.q: How much of the work can be done remotely?
faq.a: Most of it. Document review, drafting and personnel-file work happen remotely from Houston and Hyderabad. The mock office audit and the rehearsal of the witnessed demonstration are best done at your office or yard, and Atlantis sends a Level III for them.
